items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI

These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Building wa.me links that actually open the right chat
items.summary: A "Chat on WhatsApp" button looks like the easiest feature on the backlog. It's one URL. Then the bug reports come in: the link opens a "phone number shared via url is invalid" screen, or the chat opens with half the prefilled message missing. Almost every time, the cause is one of two things: the number format or the URL encoding. A click-to-chat link has two parts: https://wa.me/ ?text= The ?text= part is optional. The number is not, and it's the part people get wrong. WhatsApp wants the full international number as digits only: country code first, then the national number. No +, no 00 international prefix, no spaces, dashes or brackets. A US number written as +1 (202) 555-0123 becomes: https://wa.me/12025550123 Two traps hide here. First, 00 is a dialing prefix, not part of the number, so 0044... has to become 44.... Second, many countries use a leading trunk 0 for domestic calls. A UK mobile written locally as 07911 123456 is 447911123456 internationally. Keep that 0 after the country code and you get 4407911123456, which points to nobody. Short answer: to rate-limit OTP requests for SMS-based 2FA in Node.js, use shared backend counters in Redis or your database, enforce configurable limits per phone number and session before sending, and apply progressive backoff to repeated attempts. For password reset, reject work that cannot fit inside the remaining expiry budget. A browser countdown is feedback; the backend owns admission. items.title: Percentage calculations have 3 flavors — handling all of them in one UI
items.summary: Percentage calculations have 3 flavors — handling all of them in one UI Every percentage calculator on the web asks you to pick a mode first, and users hate that. The reason is simple: "percentage" is not one calculation. It is three different questions wearing the same % sign, and a calculator that treats them as one will quietly give the wrong answer. Here is how to handle all three in a single UI — and the edge cases that break naive implementations. The three flavors Flavor 1: What is X% of Y? The classic. 20% of an $85 bill is $17, so a 20% tip on $85 is $17 and the total is $102. Formula: Y * X / 100. Flavor 2: X is what % of Y? The comparison. $45 is what percentage of $180? 45 / 180 × 100 = 25%. Formula: X / Y * 100. Flavor 3: Percentage change. The price went from $60 to $75. That is (75 − 60) / 60 × 100 = a 25% increase. And $80 with 25% off is $80 × 0.75 = $60. Formula: (new − old) / old * 100. A single input pair (two numbers and one percentage) can serve all three if the UI labels the result instead of making the user choose a mode upfront. items.title: How a Self-Destructing Chat Room Works in the Browser – URL-Fragment Keys, AES-256-GCM and Number Matching
items.summary: End-to-end encryption solved the transport problem for chat years ago. What it did not solve is retention. An end-to-end encrypted message still sits on two phones, in a cloud backup and, sooner or later, in an export someone made for a perfectly good reason. Kriptano secure chat aims at a narrower target – a room that exists for one conversation, encrypts everything in the browser and is deleted when the time is up. This post walks through the moving parts: where the key lives, why entry uses number matching, how the room lifecycle works and how to open rooms from your own code. When the host opens a room, the browser generates a random 256-bit key and appends it to the room link after the #. Browsers do not include the fragment in HTTP requests, so the server never receives the key. Messages, participant names and files are encrypted with AES-256-GCM in each participant's browser, and the server relays and stores only ciphertext until the room ends. items.title: Turning hundreds of Japanese akiya banks into one map (politely)
items.summary: Japan has around 9 million empty houses. Hundreds of towns try to give theirs a second life through "akiya banks": municipal websites that list vacant homes, often for a few million yen. The catch for anyone outside Japan is that there is no single akiya bank. There are hundreds, each with its own markup, its own price format and its own idea of what a listing is. I'm building Engawa, an English map of those listings. This post covers what it took to turn a few dozen Japanese property sites into one catalogue of about 13,000 homes, without being a bad citizen of anyone's server. Every source gets a small adapter that knows two things: how to discover detail URLs, and how to turn a detail page into a normalized record (price in yen, land and floor area in square metres, build year, coordinates, photos). Everything else is shared. Discovered URLs go into a crawl_frontier table in SQLite (Node's built-in node:sqlite, no ORM). That one decision paid for itself many times over: a crawl can be stopped with Ctrl-C after the active batch and resumed later with --resume, failed URLs get re-queued, and a nationwide run never starts from zero. npm run crawl -- --source=ieichiba --pref=nagano

items.summary: The operational constraint decides this one: a game platform needs private tenant thumbnails that can be restored, expired, and moved to another storage provider without rewriting the game service. Short answer: make metadata part of the upload contract, then test it with a head/readback check before the thumbnail enters a retention queue. A separate metadata update call is useful for repair, but it should not be the normal write path. Infrai fits this narrow workflow when one REST contract needs to cover both the storage write and a neighboring content-processing step. The limitation is equally important: it is not suitable for public static hosting, immutable object retention, or a bulk cross-cloud migration. This is a small detail with a large blast radius. If tenant_id, snapshot_id, or content_hash disappears during upload, a list operation cannot rescue the index: object metadata is not server-searchable here, and listing filters by prefix. My concrete case is a gaming SaaS that fans out a shipment update to many subscribers. A collector's package changes from in_transit to delivered; hundreds of players may be listening for that event. I just wanted to click a .md file in Windows Explorer, press Alt+P, and see it rendered — without opening VS Code every time or installing all of PowerToys. Microsoft PowerToys previews Markdown in Explorer, but it skips Mermaid diagrams and math (and blocks images by default). items.title: Modern C# Features Look Like Syntax Sugar — Until You Realize They Change How You Design Software (.NET 11 / C# 15 Edition)
items.summary: Most developers upgrade .NET the same way. They change one line: net11.0 The build passes. The tests pass. The pull request gets approved. Nothing else changes. And that is exactly the problem. Because the code still looks like C# from five years ago: object return types that could be anything switch expressions that end in _ => throw Backing fields written by hand just to validate one value Boolean flags to escape nested loops Null checks wrapped around single assignments A full project created just to run a 20-line script All of it compiles. All of it works. And all of it ignores what the compiler can now do for you. At that moment, a critical realization emerges: New syntax is not the point. New guarantees are. .NET 11 shipped on November 10, 2026, with C# 15. .NET 10, with C# 14, is the current LTS. .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support the same day .NET 11 arrived. If your mental model of C# stopped at .NET 8, it is now officially out of support too. Modern C# features are not shortcuts. They are guarantees. items.title: MDX – Markdown Meets React Components
items.summary: Originally published with interactive examples at lukiluki.me. You are writing technical documentation in Markdown. Plain text works until the reader needs a calculator, a live example or a reusable warning box. Copying HTML fragments across articles makes them harder to maintain. How can a document stay readable while using the same components as the application? MDX combines Markdown with JSX, so documents can import and render React components. In the Next.js App Router, local MDX can participate in server rendering while interactive components live behind explicit client boundaries. This makes shared styling and focused interaction possible. The result still depends on the imported components: using MDX alone does not guarantee static output, type-safe metadata or zero client JavaScript. Merksatz (Key takeaway): The MDX compiler turns a document into JavaScript that renders React elements. Headings and paragraphs become elements; imported components appear where they are used in the document. items.title: Keep heavy React components out of the main chunk with react-view-import
items.summary: My next project needed a fully static output, but most of its work happened on the client side. The client judged the site by its Google page-performance score, so the first load had to stay as light as possible. The usual lazy-loading options did not give me what I needed. In my static export setup, a lazily loaded component still weighed on the first load. I wanted something more direct: the component is excluded from the main chunk, the site manifest keeps only a reference to it, and the chunk is fetched through a network request when a condition is met. I could not find a solution that did this, so I built react-view-import. It is standalone, with no runtime dependencies. It uses only the React that your app already has. You write the import as a function, () => import("./HeavyChart"). The build puts the component into its own chunk and leaves only a reference in the site manifest. On the page, the package renders a placeholder and watches it with an IntersectionObserver. When the condition is true, the package runs the import, the browser fetches the chunk, and the real component replaces the placeholder. items.title: Saving a Telegram chat's photos and videos in posting order: what I learned building a Windows app
items.summary: I wanted one folder per Telegram group with every photo and video in it, numbered in the order they were posted. Telegram's cache doesn't give you that: files sit in folders by type, with names like 5229911934_y.jpg. Telegram Desktop's "Export chat history" is closer, but it's a one-off copy split into photos/ and video_files/, and you have to export again to pick up new posts. So I built Chat Media Collector, a small Windows app that does exactly that. You pick a chat, it shows how many photos and videos there are and how much space they need, and it saves them as 0001.jpg, 0002.mp4, 0003.jpg… Run it again next week and only the new posts are added, with the next numbers. This post is about the parts that turned out more interesting to build than I expected. .NET 8 and WPF: one window, plus a tray icon for scheduled syncs WTelegramClient for Telegram's MTProto API. QRCoder for the "scan this with Telegram on your phone" sign-in An MSIX package for the Microsoft Store The core promise is that 0041.jpg is the 41st photo or video in the chat, today and after every later run. items.title: Simplifying modular monolith composition in .NET
items.summary: A layered .NET application splits code by technical role: endpoints in one project, handlers in another, the domain model and data access in their own. Adding a field to an order touches all four. Vertical slices split the same code by feature. Everything orders needs, from the endpoint to the query, sits together, and the change stays in one place. A modular monolith groups slices into modules and puts boundaries between them that a build can check. Orders may call billing through billing's public contract, but not read its tables or use its internal classes, and an architecture test fails if it tries. It still ships from one codebase, as one application or a handful of processes. Those tests cover the modules and exempt the host. The host references every module, because something has to register them, and it decides which ones each process runs. In every setup I've built, that decision was a side effect of something else: which projects a host referenced, what a mediator found in an assembly, what a shared AddX() helper pulled in, which if branches matched a flag. items.title: Make the agent use the existing Dialog primitive, not a new fixed overlay
items.summary: The PR adds a confirm step as a fixed inset-0 backdrop and a centered . The repo already has a Dialog (or Modal) primitive with a portal, focus trap, Escape to close, scroll lock, and a labelled title. The new overlay does not restore focus, does not close on Escape, and sits under the toast root or above the wrong z-index layer. I’ve started treating a homemade overlay as incomplete when a Dialog primitive exists. The markup is the easy part. The focus and layering are why the primitive is there. A “modal” in a tutorial is a fixed div and a button. The model can write that without finding components/Dialog. Your primitive may be named Modal, Drawer, or a Radix/Headless UI wrapper, which is easy to miss if the prompt only says “add a confirm popup.” You also skip things reviewers only catch later: initial focus on the primary action, return focus to the opener, aria-modal, and the existing reduced-motion path. items.title: Building a multi-tenant SaaS foundation on .NET 10 and Blazor: 5 decisions that mattered
items.summary: Over the last few weeks I built ShipBlazor, a starter kit for SaaS products on .NET 10. Here are the five decisions that mattered most, with the reasoning, so you can reuse them in your own projects. Make tenant isolation the default, not a habit A global query filter keyed on the current organization, automatic stamping of new rows, and a SaveChanges check that throws on cross-tenant writes. With no organization set, queries return nothing. You can’t forget a where clause you never have to write. Treat payment webhooks as unreliable Stripe can send events twice or out of order. Store processed event ids, ignore events older than the last one applied, and never trust a webhook without checking its signature. One service per feature owns the side effects Pages and the API call the same service, which writes the activity log and publishes outgoing webhooks. Nothing gets audited in one place and forgotten in another. Charge for AI before you call the model Record the request first, call the model, and delete the record if it fails. items.title: Vercel AI SDK for Beginners: Build AI Features Into Your App the React Way
items.summary: Adding a chatbot to a React app used to mean hand-writing fetch calls, streaming logic, and state updates. The Vercel AI SDK turns that into a hook. It works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers through one consistent API, so you can switch models without rewriting your UI. "use client"; import { useChat } from "ai/react"; export default function Chat() { const { messages, input, handleInputChange, handleSubmit } = useChat(); return ( {messages.map((m) => ( {m.role}: {m.content} ))} Send ); } The hook handles streaming, so the AI's reply appears word by word, and messages always holds the conversation. On the server, a route handler streams the model's response back with a few lines of code. The SDK is for you if you are building AI features — chat, text generation, structured output — into a React or Next.js app and you want the UI plumbing handled for you. It also supports tools, so the model can call your functions, and it has helpers for generating objects that match a schema. But know its limits. items.title: Why Squirix shed its web stack
items.summary: Why Squirix shed its web stack The first versions of Squirix, a distributed cache for .NET, ran as an ASP.NET Core app. Kestrel accepted connections, and a shared .proto file told the C# client and server how to talk to each other over gRPC. That saved me time when I was working out which replica could safely acknowledge a write. For 0.2.0-preview.1, I wanted to look at a cheaper operation: reading a short string that's already in memory. Even on a cache hit, the server has to decode the request, look up the key and send the value back. I wanted to be able to change how Squirix did that last part, right down to when it flushed the connection. The change happened in stages. For a while, Squirix was running a binary protocol over TLS, hosted by Kestrel, with Protobuf still encoding the messages. The SDK was the first piece to move off gRPC. Consider what happens when four small reads finish on the same connection. If all four replies are ready, the server can write them into the output buffer and flush once. items.title: Free currency rates in SwiftUI without an API key: a fallback chain with an offline cache
items.summary: A currency converter is only as reliable as its exchange rate API, and free APIs are not very reliable. Free tiers have monthly limits. Some need a key you have to ship inside the app. Some go down for an afternoon. When that happens, a converter shows a spinner, then an error, and the user deletes the app. Here is the pattern I use in Swap+, my SwiftUI currency and VAT app with 154 currencies. It has three layers: A chain of providers, tried in order, so one failing source is invisible to the user. A short-lived cache, so we don't hit any API more than we need to. An offline floor: the last good rates, or bundled defaults, so the app always opens with numbers. Instead of hard-coding one API, each source is a small config value with a priority: struct APIConfig { let name: String let baseURL: String let apiKey: String // empty for free, keyless sources let priority: Int // lower runs first var requiresKey = false // true for paid providers } The keyless sources are the interesting part. These worked without any key when I built the app (check each one's terms before you rely on it): Source Endpoint Notes Frankfurter api.frankfurter.app ECB data, about 30 major currencies FloatRates

items.title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
items.summary: We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding. To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks. Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit): - DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6 - Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4 - AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0 - MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6 - RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9 Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below (3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS): - 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7 - 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8 - 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8 Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp) Feedback and questions welcome. items.title: Best Practices for Protecting Sensitive Information and Building User Trust When Your App Goes to the Background
items.summary: This article is an English version of an article I contributed to the official pamphlet of iOSDC Japan 2026 (iOS Developers Conference Japan 2026). Have you ever thought about what your app should do when it moves to the background? The moment a user leaves your app, iOS saves a snapshot of its screen. If that snapshot shows sensitive information, someone nearby could see it when the user casually opens the App Switcher. iOS also keeps these snapshots on the device. Regular apps can't access them, but they could potentially be extracted from a jailbroken device. Apple's documentation states that apps should remove sensitive information when they enter the background. If you skip this step, users' personal information can be exposed without anyone meaning to. This article collects practical know-how, from choosing an approach to the implementation details, including two things that are easy to miss: the keyboard and permission alerts. Apple's official documentation includes the following guideline: Your app's UI must not contain any sensitive user information, such as passwords or credit card numbers. items.summary: Most real iOS projects in 2026 should run both Swift Testing and XCTest: Swift Testing for new and migrated unit tests, and XCTest for UI tests, performance tests, and any code that still interacts with Objective-C. This article details the differences between the two frameworks and guides you through migrating a production app module piece by piece without rewriting the entire suite. Each code example is from a small Swift package (AuthKit, source on GitHub) that I tested before publishing. Toolchain: Xcode 26.3 (17C529), Swift 6.2.4, Swift 6 language mode. Platforms: macOS, plus the iOS 26.2 and iOS 18.5 simulators. Result: 22 Swift tests (38 test cases once arguments are expanded) and 5 XCTest tests, all in one package with no warnings. Where a feature needs a particular Swift version, I say so. Modern iOS code is concurrent by default. A sign-in flow might involve a @MainActor view model, an actor handling the session, and a Sendable network client—all triggered with a single tap. Swift 6's strict concurrency checking identifies many data races during compilation. items.title: A Timer Is Not a Clock: What We Learned Building a Time Tracker for Windows, Mac and Linux
items.summary: Counting seconds sounds like the easiest program in the world. Start a timer, add one every second, show the number. We build TimoDesk, a time tracker for remote teams: a desktop app that tracks time on tasks, takes screenshots at set intervals, measures keyboard and mouse activity, and syncs it all to a web dashboard. After shipping it on three platforms, we can say this with confidence: counting seconds is the hardest part of the whole product. This is our first post here, so instead of a feature tour, here are the lessons that cost us the most to learn. TimoDesk started as a single Electron app. Today it is three: Windows: .NET (WPF) Mac: Swift and SwiftUI Linux: Electron We moved Windows and Mac to native code because a time tracker lives in the background all day. It hooks the keyboard and mouse, captures the screen, and wakes up every second. On those two platforms, native code gave us lower memory use, better system integration and fewer surprises with permissions and sleep. items.title: Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions'
items.summary: "A handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets," warn two security developers at the Python Software Foundation. Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents? Yes, repeatedly... The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one... When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one. pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway... Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises. The issue_comment trigger

items.title: I stress-tested my Mac media player with 400 Mbps 4K files — here's what happened
items.summary: Specs lie. "Supports 4K" can mean anything from buttery playback to a slideshow with fan noise. So before I called SilkPlayer — my free, native macOS media player — ready, I ran it through the files I actually worry about: the Jellyfish 4K HEVC 10-bit stress files at 120, 200 and 400 Mbps, plus 8K Dolby Vision in Profile 5 and Profile 8.4. The setup is deliberately unglamorous: SilkPlayer 2.0.2, Metal hardware decode, zero-copy to the display. No server, no transcoding, no tricks. The files play straight from local storage. All five passed. The 400 Mbps file — several times the bitrate of a 4K Blu-ray — played smooth. The 8K Dolby Vision Profile 5 file showed the colors right, which is the part most Mac players get wrong: Profile 5 stores its color reshaping data in the RPU metadata, and players that ignore it show purple or washed-out frames. SilkPlayer's Profile 5 pipeline is developed in-house, RPU parsing included. I'm not claiming the player is bulletproof. These five tests cover the decode path only. items.title: Turning raw iPhone and Mac screen recordings into 1080p app demos offline
items.summary: Recording a 15-second screen clip of a new iPhone or Mac feature is fast. Turning that raw .mov into something clean enough for a changelog or social post usually takes much longer: trimming the Control Center pull-down at the end, cutting out a four-second loading pause, and zooming into the small button you tapped so phone viewers can actually read it. I built TapZoom to do that cleanup on a single screen, running natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac without uploading footage to a cloud editor. On iOS, app sandboxing prevents one app from reading raw touch coordinates recorded inside another app. Instead of pretending to capture hidden system touches, TapZoom runs a fast on-device frame-difference pass over the video (ignoring the top status bar clock) and places visual Screen Change Cues along the timeline wherever the UI updates. You can jump straight from cue to cue, step frame by frame, and tap directly on the preview canvas to drop a zoom highlight (Snappy, Smooth, or Gentle) and a high-contrast tap ripple. items.title: iOS privacy policy generator — what to use, and what App Review asks of it
items.summary: You search "iOS privacy policy generator" because Apple won't let you submit your app without one, and you don't want to write 1,500 words of legalese from scratch. The first ten Google results are generic privacy-policy SaaS tools — Termly, iubenda, TermsFeed, Get Terms, plus a long tail of free templates. Most of them weren't built with App Review in mind. Not because the legal content is wrong. It's usually fine. The gap is that your privacy policy has to agree with three other things — your Info.plist permission strings, your App Privacy Details questionnaire in App Store Connect, and your PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file — and a generic generator has no idea what any of those say. So your policy ends up declaring data practices that don't match what your app actually does. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.
